name: Suresh
definition: Suresh is a composite portrait of a middle-aged areca trader and commission agent working in Holenarasipura taluk, Hassan district, situated in the Malnad areca belt where grading, pricing and market intelligence shape daily life. He represents households that straddle agriculture and trade, earning from both their own small holdings and the margins they secure as intermediaries in the areca economy.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Suresh owns four acres of areca plantation near Holenarasipura town and operates as a commission agent in the town's areca market, grading and brokering loads brought in by smallholders from surrounding villages. His working day begins at dawn with a walk through his own plantation, checking for Koleroga fruit rot and Yellow Leaf Disease symptoms, then shifts to the market shed by eight o'clock where farmers unload sacks and haggle over moisture content and grade. He earns a two-to-three-percent commission on each transaction and also buys small lots outright when prices dip, holding them in a rented godown until rates improve. Income varies sharply with the harvest calendar and national areca prices, which have swung between ₹25,000 and ₹45,000 per quintal in recent years. Mobile apps now broadcast real-time prices from Mangaluru and Sirsi, tightening margins and forcing him to judge quality by touch and sight faster than younger traders scrolling phones. Expenses include godown rent, lorry hire for his own crop, pesticide and fertiliser for the plantation, and repayments on a ₹4 lakh loan taken from the district milk union's credit arm three years ago to expand storage space.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Suresh lives in a tile-roofed house on the edge of Holenarasipura town with his wife Savitha, who manages the household and keeps accounts for the trading business, their two sons aged nineteen and sixteen, and his widowed mother. Savitha's literacy and numeracy allow her to track commission slips and godown stock, a partnership Suresh credits for keeping the business transparent when disputes arise. Their elder son completed second-year PUC in Holenarasipura and now works as a sales assistant in a mobile-phone shop in Hassan town, sending ₹3,000 home each month but resisting any talk of returning to areca trading. The younger son is in first-year PUC at the same government college Suresh attended. His mother, in her late sixties, suffers from diabetes and high blood pressure, requiring monthly doctor visits in Hassan. Gender roles in the household follow a practical division: Savitha handles indoor work, market accounts and all interactions with women farmers who prefer dealing with her; Suresh handles field labour, godown management and lorry logistics. The family's marriage and caste networks tie them to other Vokkaliga farming and trading families across Holenarasipura and Channarayapatna taluks.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Suresh studied up to tenth standard in Holenarasipura's government high school in the late 1990s, then discontinued after his father's sudden death forced him into managing the family plantation and trading work. He regrets not completing PUC, believing it would have given him confidence in bank negotiations and government-scheme paperwork. His elder son finished second PUC with modest marks—enough to avoid repeating the year but not enough for a veterinary or engineering seat—and chose immediate employment over a BCom course, citing the cost and uncertain job prospects. The younger son is studying in the science stream at the government PUC college in Holenarasipura, hoping for a pharmacy diploma or a BSc that might lead to a government job, though his father quietly doubts the feasibility. School fees are low—around ₹500 per year for PUC—but hostel and coaching expenses in Hassan would add ₹30,000 annually, a sum Suresh is unwilling to spend unless his son's grades improve. The family hopes education will spare the younger boy the weather-dependence and price volatility that define areca trading, but neither son has shown interest in taking over the plantation.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Suresh's own health is generally sound, though he experiences chronic lower-back pain from years of lifting areca sacks and occasional breathlessness he attributes to pesticide exposure during spraying seasons. He consults a private GP in Holenarasipura for the back pain and takes over-the-counter painkillers rather than traveling to Hassan for scans he considers unnecessary. His mother's diabetes and hypertension require monthly check-ups at the government taluk hospital and a regimen of tablets that cost roughly ₹800 per month; the family enrolled her in Ayushman Bharat two years ago, which covered a brief hospitalisation for uncontrolled blood sugar but does not reduce the monthly medicine bill. Savitha's health is stable, though she complains of joint pain and fatigue during the peak areca harvest when she works long market hours alongside him. The household's main health anxieties centre on his mother's age and the risk of a stroke or kidney failure, scenarios they have seen among neighbours and that would exhaust savings quickly. Water quality in their locality is acceptable—piped supply from the town system—but during summer the tap runs dry for hours and they rely on a borewell, which Suresh suspects carries higher nitrate levels from surrounding fertiliser runoff. Snakebite and pesticide poisoning are recognised risks in the plantation, and Suresh keeps a basic first-aid kit and the number of the taluk hospital's casualty ward.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Suresh belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant farming and landowning group in Hassan district, and his family's social and economic networks are embedded in caste ties that shape credit access, marriage alliances and market trust. He is not outwardly religious but observes major festivals—Ugadi, Deepavali, Varamahalakshmi—and makes an annual visit to the Shravanabelagola Gomateshwara temple, more for family tradition than personal devotion. His wife is more devout, keeping a small puja corner in the house and fasting on Thursdays. Community ties matter practically: when his godown roof collapsed during heavy rain two years ago, it was fellow Vokkaliga traders who lent him tarpaulins and labour without formal agreement, and when his elder son needed a job reference, a cousin's husband in Hassan provided it. The local Farmers' Association, dominated by areca and coconut growers, is the arena where Suresh hears about new government schemes, price-support demands and pesticide-dealer complaints. He attends its monthly meetings irregularly but values the collective bargaining power it claims to wield with the Agriculture Department. Social hierarchy is felt but rarely discussed openly: he deals daily with Dalit labourers who load sacks in the market, Muslim traders who handle some of the Mangaluru export logistics, and Havyaka Brahmin growers from the ghat taluks whose areca he grades as premium quality, all within unspoken but understood boundaries of caste and economic power.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Suresh's encounters with government revolve around the Agriculture Department's pesticide subsidies, the district milk union's credit schemes and the taluk panchayat's market-infrastructure promises. He took a ₹4 lakh loan from the milk union's self-help-group-linked credit programme three years ago at nine-percent interest, finding it faster and less document-heavy than a nationalised bank, and has repaid on schedule. He applied once for a Kisan Credit Card but was deterred by the paperwork and the bank officer's insistence on updated land records, which required a surveyor's visit he could not afford to wait for. His areca plantation is registered under the Horticulture Department's area-expansion scheme, which provided a small subsidy for drip-irrigation pipes he installed five years ago, though the pipes clogged within two seasons and he reverted to flood irrigation. The taluk panchayat promised a covered areca-market shed with weigh-bridge and grading facilities in 2021; construction began but stalled, leaving half-built walls that now shelter stray cattle. Suresh has attended two public meetings on the Kasturirangan ESA notification, organized by the Farmers' Association in 2026, and signed a petition opposing land-use restrictions, though he does not expect his four-acre holding to be directly affected. He distrusts the forest department, which he believes prioritises elephants over farmers' livelihoods, and he has heard of—but not personally received—compensation delays for elephant-damaged areca in neighbouring Alur taluk.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Suresh worries most about areca price volatility and the diseases—Koleroga and Yellow Leaf—spreading faster than the Horticulture Department's advisory can contain, a combination that could wipe out a season's income and trap him in debt. He is proud of his ability to judge areca quality by eye and of the respect his fair dealing has earned among smallholders who return to his shed year after year, but he fears that younger traders armed with apps and direct WhatsApp links to Mangaluru exporters will undercut his margins and render his experience obsolete. He feels a deep ambivalence about his sons' futures: relief that his elder boy has escaped the farm-trade grind and found salaried work, but also disappointment that neither son values the land or the business enough to continue it, leaving the question of succession unresolved. He blames state neglect—poor roads that damage areca loads in transit, delayed crop insurance payouts, the unfulfilled market-shed promise—for making farming and trading unattractive to the young, and he points to the steady trickle of neighbours' children leaving for Bengaluru and Hassan as proof. He holds the forest department responsible for the growing elephant menace in Alur and surrounding areas, arguing that compensation is too slow and too small to cover real losses. He respects the Hoysala heritage that draws tourists to Hassan but sees little economic benefit reaching his taluk, where infrastructure lags behind Hassan town. He demands better crop insurance that pays promptly, a functional market with weigh-bridge and covered storage, and an areca price-support mechanism that reflects input costs rather than leaving growers at the mercy of Mangaluru's export demand swings. He views the Kasturirangan ESA restrictions as a Bengaluru-imposed threat to small farmers' land rights, though he acknowledges in private that some regulation of pesticide runoff and forest-edge expansion might protect the water and soil his sons will not inherit.
